lesson.title: Dominant and Recessive Alleles: When One Version Wins Out
lesson.summary: When an individual carries two different alleles for a gene, a dominant allele produces its associated trait regardless of what the other allele is, while a recessive allele's trait is only visible when both copies present are the recessive version.
lesson.body:
When an individual is heterozygous, carrying two different alleles for a gene, one of those alleles often determines the observable trait on its own, while the other has no visible effect at all. The allele whose trait shows up is called dominant, and the allele whose trait is hidden is called recessive. Returning to the Pp example from the law of segregation chapter, a Pp plant shows purple flowers, exactly like a PP plant, because the purple allele, P, is dominant over the white allele, p. The recessive white trait stays hidden whenever at least one P allele is present, and it only becomes visible when both alleles present are the recessive version, as in a pp plant.

It helps to have at least a basic sense of why this happens. Many genes carry the instructions for making a particular protein, and a dominant allele frequently produces a working copy of that protein, for instance an enzyme involved in making pigment. Often, just one working copy is enough to produce the associated trait, which is why a single dominant allele can mask a recessive one. A recessive allele frequently fails to produce a fully functional version of that protein, so its effect only becomes visible when there is no working copy at all to compensate for it. This is a useful general picture, but it is worth flagging that not every gene follows this simple, full dominance pattern. Some genes show other relationships between alleles, such as one allele only partially masking the other. The full dominance pattern described here, though, is the one Mendel worked with in his pea experiments and the one this chapter, and the examples that follow it, focus on.

The same Pp by Pp cross used earlier shows dominance clearly. PP, homozygous dominant, and Pp, heterozygous, both produce purple flowers, since one copy of P is enough. Only pp, homozygous recessive, produces white flowers. Working through the same cross as before, the genotype ratio among the offspring is 1 PP to 2 Pp to 1 pp, but because PP and Pp look identical due to dominance, the phenotype ratio comes out to 3 purple to 1 white. That 3 to 1 ratio is a direct signature of dominance at work, two of the three genotype categories collapse into a single visible outcome.

This also reveals something worth carrying forward: PP and Pp are genetically different individuals that happen to look identical. Telling apart what an organism's genes actually are from what trait it visibly displays becomes essential once dominance is involved, which is exactly the distinction covered next, between genotype and phenotype.
